name: Anterior thalamic nucleus
function: Limbic relay of the Papez circuit: it receives hippocampal information via the mammillary bodies (mammillothalamic tract) and projects to the cingulate gyrus, gating episodic memory encoding and spatial navigation. Damage disconnects the Papez loop and reproduces a dense amnestic state.

afferent: Mammillary bodies via the mammillothalamic tract (tract of Vicq d'Azyr)
Indirect hippocampal input through the mammillary bodies (mammillothalamic tract); a minor direct subicular projection to the anterior nuclei is described experimentally but is not the defining route
efferent: Cingulate gyrus (Brodmann areas 23, 24, 32) via the anterior limb of the internal capsule
Reciprocal projections to the mammillary bodies and prefrontal cortex

bloodSupply: PCA — tuberothalamic (anterior thalamoperforating) artery, arising from the P1 segment or the posterior communicating artery.

clinical.findings: Acute anterograde amnesia, apathy, abulia and executive dysfunction; left-sided lesions add an 'aphasia-plus' state and right-sided lesions neglect, because the Papez circuit is interrupted at the anterior nucleus.
Thiamine deficiency damages the anterior thalamic nuclei together with the mammillary bodies, producing dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Limbic System: Homeostasis, Olfaction, Memory, and Emotion'

name: Ventral anterior nucleus (VA)
function: Motor gating hub of the basal-ganglia thalamocortical loop: pallidal (GPi) and substantia nigra pars reticulata output relays here before reaching premotor and supplementary motor cortex, shaping motor readiness and movement initiation.

afferent: Globus pallidus internus via the ansa lenticularis and the lenticular (H2) / thalamic (H1) fasciculi
Premotor and supplementary motor cortex feedback
efferent: Premotor cortex (area 6) and supplementary motor area via the anterior limb of the internal capsule
Frontal eye field region (magnocellular medial VA)

bloodSupply: Tuberothalamic (anterior thalamoperforating) artery rostrally; paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches of the PCA medially.

clinical.findings: Infarction involving VA disconnects pallidal output from the motor thalamus, adding motor-programming and initiation deficits (abulia, loss of spontaneous action) to the amnestic-apathic syndrome.
Acute inability to stand after rostral thalamic (VA-involving) lesions, with active pushing and falls but no weakness or cerebellar signs to explain them.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Basal Ganglia'

name: Ventral lateral nucleus (VL)
function: Cerebellar and pallidal relay to the primary motor cortex: the oral posterior (cerebellar) division receives the crossed dentatothalamic fibers of the superior cerebellar peduncle and calibrates the timing and amplitude of voluntary movement. The ventral intermediate (VIM) zone is the stereotactic target for tremor suppression.

afferent: Contralateral dentate (and interposed) nuclei via the superior cerebellar peduncle and its decussation
Globus pallidus internus via the thalamic fasciculus (H1)
efferent: Primary motor cortex (area 4) and premotor/supplementary motor areas via the posterior limb of the internal capsule

bloodSupply: Thalamogeniculate artery (caudal VL) and tuberothalamic artery (rostral VL), branches of the PCA.

clinical.findings: VL infarction disconnects the dentatothalamocortical loop, producing contralateral intention tremor, dysmetria and ataxic gait; the same circuit is the target of VIM thalamotomy/DBS for Parkinsonian and essential tremor.
clinical.note: cerebellar-type signs from a thalamic lesion: the dentatothalamic relay, not the cerebellum itself, is interrupted

clinical.syndrome: Ataxic hemiparesis from a thalamic lacune
clinical.findings: A small thalamogeniculate infarct can involve VL together with the adjacent posterior-limb fibres of the internal capsule, giving mild contralateral weakness with out-of-proportion limb ataxia, and trunk instability severe enough to prevent standing (thalamic astasia); at the bedside the picture is indistinguishable from a pontine or capsular lacune.
clinical.note: Ataxic hemiparesis is a syndrome of site, not of cause: identical presentations arise from lacunes in the internal capsule, basis pontis and thalamus, so imaging decides the level.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Basal Ganglia'

name: Ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL)
function: Obligatory thalamic relay of body somatosensation: medial-lemniscal (touch, vibration, joint-position) and spinothalamic (pain, temperature) fibers terminate in a somatotopic map — leg lateral, arm medial — and project to primary somatosensory cortex. Small-hole lesions here cause contralateral hemianesthesia and are the classic substrate of central post-stroke pain.

afferent: Medial lemniscus (contralateral dorsal column-medial lemniscus system: vibration, proprioception, discriminative touch)
efferent: Primary somatosensory cortex (S1, areas 3, 1, 2) via the posterior limb of the internal capsule
Secondary somatosensory cortex and insular nociceptive matrix

bloodSupply: PCA — thalamogeniculate artery (branch of the P2 segment).

clinical.findings: After a thalamogeniculate infarct, initial contralateral hemisensory loss evolves weeks to months later into severe burning pain with allodynia and hyperpathia; see the syndrome browser entry.
A lacune confined to VPL/VPM causes contralateral face-arm-leg hemianesthesia without weakness; proprioceptive loss may add sensory ataxia and transient choreoathetosis.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Somatosensory Pathways'

name: Ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM)
function: Thalamic relay for the face and head: the trigeminal lemniscus delivers contralateral facial touch, pain and temperature, the dorsal trigeminothalamic tract adds ipsilateral oral mechanosensation, and the parvocellular medial pole (VPMpc) relays taste to the insular and frontal opercular cortex.

afferent: Contralateral ventral trigeminothalamic (trigeminal lemniscus) tract from the principal sensory and spinal trigeminal nuclei
Solitariothalamic taste fibers to VPMpc via the central tegmental tract
efferent: Face region of primary somatosensory cortex (lateral postcentral gyrus, areas 3, 1, 2)
Insular and frontal opercular taste cortex (VPMpc)

bloodSupply: PCA — thalamogeniculate artery; paramedian (artery of Percheron) perforators contribute medially.

clinical.findings: Pain and hypesthesia restricted to the contralateral corner of the mouth and the hand from small VPM/VPL-border infarcts — the somatotopic lips-beside-hand representation of the ventrobasal complex.
VPM lesions give hemifacial loss of touch, pain and temperature with a preserved corneal reflex arc; taste is lost when VPMpc is involved.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Somatosensory Pathways'

name: Lateral dorsal nucleus
function: Dorsal-tier limbic association nucleus continuous with the anterior nuclear group: it links hippocampal and pretectal inputs to cingulate and parietal cortex, participating in memory retrieval and spatial-attention circuitry.

afferent: Cingulate and parietal association cortex feedback
efferent: Cingulate gyrus and superior parietal association cortex (areas 5, 7)
Reciprocal projections to the hippocampal formation

bloodSupply: Posterior choroidal (medial and lateral) and thalamogeniculate branches of the PCA.

clinical.findings: Isolated LD infarcts are rare; LD involvement in larger posterior-choroidal strokes contributes to memory impairment and contralateral spatial neglect.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Limbic System: Homeostasis, Olfaction, Memory, and Emotion'

name: Lateral posterior nucleus
function: Parietal-association relay behind the lateral dorsal nucleus: with the pulvinar it integrates superior-colliculus visual signals with somatosensory association input and projects to parietal cortex, supporting visuospatial attention and orienting.

efferent: Superior parietal association cortex (areas 5 and 7)
Cingulate cortex

bloodSupply: PCA — posterior choroidal and thalamogeniculate branches.

clinical.findings: Right-sided LP/pulvinar lesions impair assignment of stimulus salience and contralateral visual attention, mimicking parietal neglect without cortical damage.
clinical.vascular: PCA — posterior choroidal or thalamogeniculate branches

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'

name: Pulvinar
function: Largest thalamic nucleus and a hub of visual attention: it connects extrastriate, inferotemporal and parietal association cortex with the superior colliculus, assigning behavioral salience to stimuli and coordinating eye-hand orienting; its posterior (limbic) nuclei also forward spinothalamic nociceptive traffic.

afferent: Superior colliculus via the brachium of the superior colliculus
efferent: Extrastriate visual and inferotemporal association cortex
Superior parietal lobule, prefrontal and cingulate cortex

bloodSupply: PCA — thalamogeniculate artery and lateral posterior choroidal artery; the whole pulvinar is PCA territory (the middle cerebral artery never supplies the thalamus; the anterior choroidal artery is the only non-PCA contributor to the thalamus).

clinical.findings: Pulvinar and posterior-group involvement in thalamogeniculate infarcts contributes to central post-stroke pain and proprioceptive ataxia; see the syndrome browser entry.

clinical.syndrome: Homonymous visual attention and field deficits
clinical.findings: Pulvinar lesions give incongruous homonymous field loss or visual inattention; bilateral damage can produce Balint-like simultanagnosia with preserved acuity.
clinical.vascular: PCA — posterior choroidal or thalamogeniculate branches

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Visual System'

name: Mediodorsal nucleus (MD)
function: Executive relay of the thalamus: the mediodorsal nucleus reciprocally connects the amygdala and temporal limbic cortex with dorsolateral prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex — also carrying nigral and collicular inputs — supporting working memory, decision-making, affective valuation and memory retrieval.

afferent: Superior colliculus (caudal MD) and olfactory-related input
efferent: Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (area 46) and orbitofrontal cortex via the anterior limb of the internal capsule
Reciprocal prefrontal projections back to MD

bloodSupply: PCA — paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches including the artery of Percheron when present; anterior choroidal contributions rostrolaterally.

clinical.findings: Bilateral MD and midline infarction produces abrupt hypersomnia, vertical gaze palsy, dense anterograde amnesia and apathy; see the syndrome browser entry.
Thiamine-deficiency injury to the mediodorsal nuclei (with the mammillary bodies) underlies the confabulatory amnestic state.
MD lesions disconnect prefrontal cortex and mimic frontal syndromes: abulia with loss of spontaneous speech (medial/lateral MD) or disinhibition with orbitofrontal-pole involvement.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Limbic System: Homeostasis, Olfaction, Memory, and Emotion'

name: Centromedian-parafascicular nuclei
function: Intralaminar system embedded in the internal medullary lamina: centromedian closes striatal-motor loops (pallidal input, striatal and motor-cortical output), while parafascicular — with the midline nuclei — forms the thalamic arm of the ascending reticular activating system; the rostral intralaminar group (central lateral, paracentral, central medial) is not covered by this record and relays the medial (arousal-affective) pain system.

afferent: Brainstem reticular formation: cholinergic (PPT/LDT) and monoaminergic arousal systems
efferent: Striatum (putamen and caudate) plus motor and premotor cortex (centromedian)
Widespread cortex, limbic system and brainstem arousal targets (parafascicular and midline projection system)

bloodSupply: PCA — paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches, including the artery of Percheron when present.

clinical.findings: Bilateral CM-PF and MD injury causes hypersomnia or coma at onset with subsequent inattention, memory disturbance and vertical gaze palsy.
Parafascicular and posterior-group involvement contributes to burning dysesthetic pain after deep thalamic strokes.
clinical.note: centromedian DBS is used experimentally for refractory epilepsy and disorders of consciousness

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Somatosensory Pathways'

name: Midline (paraventricular) thalamic nuclei
function: Midline limbic nuclei on the walls of the third ventricle (paraventricular, rhomboid, reuniens groups): they connect hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray and amygdala with limbic cortex, mediating nonspecific arousal, stress responsiveness and autonomic-endocrine integration.

afferent: Periaqueductal gray and brainstem reticular formation
efferent: Anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex
Amygdala, hippocampus and entorhinal cortex (reciprocal)

bloodSupply: PCA — paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches; posterior choroidal arteries caudally.

clinical.findings: Midline nuclear involvement in Percheron-territory infarcts contributes to hypersomnia, apathy, memory deficits and autonomic instability.

clinical.syndrome: Disorders of consciousness from bilateral paramedian thalamic damage
clinical.findings: The midline and intralaminar nuclei form the thalamic arm of the ascending arousal system, so bilateral injury — Percheron-territory infarction, thalamic haemorrhage or Wernicke encephalopathy — can leave coma, hypersomnia, akinetic mutism or a 'thalamic dementia' with severe anterograde amnesia and apathy, while the EEG shows diffuse slowing and the cortex looks structurally intact on imaging.
clinical.vascular: PCA — paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches, including a shared artery of Percheron
clinical.note: One Percheron trunk can supply both medial thalami, so a single small-vessel occlusion produces bilateral disease — the reason the thalamus must be inspected in any undiagnosed coma or hypersomnia.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Limbic System: Homeostasis, Olfaction, Memory, and Emotion'

name: Thalamic reticular nucleus
function: A thin GABAergic shell wrapping the lateral thalamus: the reticular nucleus receives collaterals of every corticothalamic and thalamocortical axon and returns inhibition to the relay nuclei, gating sensory traffic, generating sleep spindles and slow-wave rhythms, and implementing attentional filtering.

afferent: Basal forebrain and brainstem cholinergic, serotonergic and noradrenergic modulators
efferent: Inhibitory (GABAergic) projections to the dorsal thalamic relay nuclei — no cortical projection

bloodSupply: Anterior choroidal artery and thalamogeniculate/posterior choroidal branches of the PCA (lateral thalamic rim).

clinical.findings: Prion degeneration targeting the anteroventral and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei (with the inferior olive) abolishes sleep spindles and normal sleep architecture, producing progressive insomnia with dysautonomia.
clinical.note: neurodegenerative (PRNP) — the canonical human TRN/anterior-thalamus syndrome

clinical.findings: TRN burst firing through T-type calcium channels paces thalamocortical oscillations; ethosuximide blocks these channels and suppresses absence seizures.
clinical.note: physiological correlate of TRN rhythm generation

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'

name: Lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)
function: Obligatory relay of retinal vision to cortex: six layers receive a strictly retinotopic, eye-segregated map (ipsilateral eye 2/3/5, contralateral 1/4/6), with magnocellular layers serving motion and parvocellular layers form and color, forwarded to V1 via the retrolenticular internal capsule. Pupil-light-reflex fibers leave the optic tract before the LGN, so LGN lesions spare the light reflex.

afferent: Retinal ganglion cells via the optic tract (M-layers: motion; P-layers: form/color; koniocellular layers: blue-yellow)
Pulvinar, superior colliculus and brainstem attention/arousal modulators
efferent: Primary visual cortex (V1, area 17) via the retrolenticular internal capsule (optic radiations)

bloodSupply: Anterior choroidal artery (anterior and lateral LGN) and lateral posterior choroidal branch of the PCA (posterior and hilar LGN) — a dual supply.

clinical.findings: Anterior choroidal infarction of the LGN hilum gives a homonymous horizontal wedge sectoranopia; lateral posterior choroidal infarcts give the complementary horizontal sectoranopia — the dual blood supply produces mutually exclusive field patterns.
clinical.vascular: Anterior choroidal vs lateral posterior choroidal arteries

clinical.findings: LGN lesions produce incomplete, incongruous contralateral field loss with a spared pupillary light reflex — the hallmark separating LGN from optic-tract lesions.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Visual System'

name: Medial geniculate nucleus (MGN)
function: Thalamic relay of audition: the tonotopically organized medial geniculate body receives the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects through the sublenticular internal capsule to Heschl's gyrus — ventral division for frequency analysis, dorsal (polymodal) and medial divisions for sound salience, arousal and multimodal integration.

afferent: Inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus (terminal of the lateral lemniscus system)
Reticular activating system input to the medial division
efferent: Primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus, areas 41/42) via the sublenticular internal capsule (auditory radiations)

bloodSupply: PCA — thalamogeniculate branch, with anterior choroidal contributions to the medial pole.

clinical.findings: Bilateral MGN or auditory-radiation lesions abolish conscious sound perception despite normal cochlear function and intact brainstem reflexes; asymmetric lesions leave pure word deafness or nonverbal-sound agnosia.
clinical.vascular: PCA — bilateral thalamogeniculate or paramedian perforators

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'

name: Internal medullary lamina
function: Y-shaped sheet of myelinated fibers that partitions the thalamus into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear masses; the centromedian and parafascicular nuclei are embedded within its laminae, and its perforating vessels are a favored site of hypertensive thalamic hemorrhage.
contextNote: Context record: white-matter lamina tagged on plate-thalamus-mid and plate-coronal-thalamus; not a functional nucleus — see the individual thalamic nucleus records.

afferent: Intralaminar fibers of the embedded centromedian-parafascicular nuclei
Fibers crossing between the nuclear groups it separates
efferent: Intralaminar projections to striatum and widespread cortex via the embedded nuclei

bloodSupply: PCA — paramedian and thalamogeniculate perforating branches (intrathalamic perforators).

clinical.findings: Deep thalamic hemorrhages arise from perforators along the lamina and often rupture into the third ventricle; contralateral sensory loss with 'wrong-way' eye deviation is typical.
Lesions crossing the lamina injure several nuclear groups at once, explaining the combined sensory loss, arousal failure and amnesia of deep thalamic strokes.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'

name: Thalamus (context envelope)
function: Silhouette envelope of the paired thalamic ovoids — each an egg-shaped mass about 3 cm long flanking the third ventricle, joined to its partner by the interthalamic adhesion in roughly 70% of brains — used for the 3D scene and the sagittal/coronal plate blocks; the individual nuclei are separate records.
contextNote: Envelope/block tag for the thalamus silhouette on sagittal and coronal plates and in the 3D scene; not a nucleus record (see the 14 individual thalamic nucleus records).

afferent: All thalamocortical, corticothalamic, cerebellar, pallidal, retinal, auditory and somatosensory afferents listed in the individual nucleus records
efferent: Layered cortical projections through the internal capsule (see individual nuclei)

bloodSupply: PCA perforators — tuberothalamic (anterior), paramedian/Percheron (medial), thalamogeniculate (inferolateral) — plus anterior and posterior choroidal arteries laterally and posteriorly.

clinical.findings: Bilateral paramedian thalamic lesions (the envelope highlights both thalami): hypersomnia, vertical gaze palsy and amnesia; see the syndrome browser entry.
Acute thalamic lesions (often tuberothalamic territory) cause inability to maintain stance with active pushing toward the affected side, out of proportion to weakness.
